title: Getting distracted
subtitle: Why a notification costs more than a glance
question: What happens when you get interrupted?
teaser: Read a paragraph while the screen tries to take you away from it.
intro: Switching tasks is not free, and the cost is not the few seconds you looked away. It is the cost of taking apart one set of goals and building another — plus the leftovers of the first one that keep leaking into the second.

events.title: Reading
events.explanation: Reading means holding a goal, your place on the page, and a half-built sense of the sentence — all at once, all actively.

events.title: Building meaning
events.explanation: Words are being turned into meaning and fitted into a running picture of the sentence. That picture is what you lose when you look away.

events.title: Holding the thread
events.explanation: Something has to keep the task steady while everything else competes for you.

events.title: Something appears
events.explanation: Something sudden, unexpected, and possibly important. 'Possibly important' is the key part — notifications are built to pass that test.
events.science: Abrupt onsets capture attention especially effectively. Designers of notification systems did not discover this by accident.

events.title: An interrupt signal
events.explanation: A signal that your current goal might no longer be the right one. This happens whether you want it to or not.

events.title: Priority shifts
events.explanation: Priority slides toward the new thing. Your eyes may already be moving.

events.title: Two goals at once
events.explanation: Keep reading, or deal with the new thing. Both are live, and something notices the clash.

events.title: Control is increased
events.explanation: Noticing a clash is followed by trying harder. That is why the second interruption in a row feels more tiring to resist.

events.title: The configuration is rebuilt
events.explanation: Switching means loading a different set of goals and expectations. That rebuild takes time that feels like nothing is happening.
events.science: Task-switch costs appear even when the switch is fully predictable and the person has had time to prepare, which argues that part of the cost is reconfiguration itself.

events.title: Working memory takes the hit
events.explanation: The half-built sense of the sentence was only being held in mind. Nothing wrote it down. It fades.

events.title: Residue
events.explanation: The abandoned task does not shut off cleanly. Bits of it stay active and get in the way of the new one.
events.science: This carry-over is measurable as slower, more error-prone performance on the new task for some time after the switch.

events.title: Finding your place
events.explanation: You go back to the paragraph and re-read the last sentence. That re-read is the cost, made visible.

causalChain.label: A task configuration is held
causalChain.detail: Goal, place and half-built meaning are all being actively held.

causalChain.label: An abrupt event occurs
causalChain.detail: Something sudden and apparently relevant appears — the most effective combination there is.

causalChain.label: Reorienting is signalled
causalChain.detail: Reorienting is not a request. Priority starts moving.

causalChain.label: Conflict is detected
causalChain.detail: Two incompatible goals are live at the same time.

causalChain.label: Control increases
causalChain.detail: The clash triggers an adjustment that makes resisting possible, and tiring.

causalChain.label: Reconfiguration
causalChain.detail: A different set of goals gets loaded. That takes time no matter how ready you were.

causalChain.label: The old task leaks
causalChain.detail: Leftovers from the abandoned task keep interfering with the new one.

science.text: Switching between tasks produces reliable costs in speed and accuracy, even when the switch is predictable and prepared for.
Abrupt onsets and unexpected but relevant events capture attention involuntarily and engage a right-lateralised ventral network.
Response conflict is followed by measurable adjustments in subsequent control, a pattern robust across many task designs.
We draw a clean switch from one task to another. In practice the two overlap, and the interference between them is continuous rather than staged.
The 'working memory bar' depletes smoothly here. Real capacity limits are better described as interference between similar representations than as a tank emptying.
Nothing here measures your focus. The bars respond to the simulation's own parameters, which you control.

references.label: Task-switching costs
references.note: A large literature establishing that reconfiguring a task set carries measurable costs independent of time away from the task.

references.label: Attentional capture
references.note: Work on how abrupt onsets and goal-relevant features involuntarily draw attention.

references.label: Conflict monitoring and control
references.note: An influential account in which conflict signals drive subsequent increases in cognitive control.

readouts.label: On-task stability
readouts.note: How well the task you were on survives the interruption.

readouts.label: Reconfiguration cost
readouts.note: How expensive it is to rebuild. Higher is worse.

readouts.label: Interference carry-over
readouts.note: How much of the abandoned task keeps leaking into the new one.

outcome.headline: Being interrupted
outcome.body: The notification did not cost you the four seconds you spent reading it. It cost you the sentence you were holding, the time to rebuild your goal, and a stretch afterwards where the old task kept getting in the way.
outcome.insight: You cannot decide not to be interrupted. You can only decide what gets to interrupt you — and that is a decision you make beforehand, not in the moment.
